one_liner: Designers' AES-NI C code for LeMac, a nonce-based AES-round MAC about 4-7x faster than AES-128-GCM's GHASH on long messages.
what_it_does: This is the reference code for LeMac and PetitMac, two 128-bit-key, 128-bit-nonce, 128-bit-tag MACs from ToSC 2024(2). They are built from a new AES-round universal hash plus the EWCDM nonce-based construction. lemac.c exposes lemac_init(ctx, key) and a one-shot lemac_MAC(ctx, nonce, msg, len, tag); petitmac.c has the same shape. A Python model and test-vector script and a Linux benchmark suite with about 12 competing MACs and AEADs come with it. It authenticates only and does no encryption, and its tags are unrelated to GCM or GMAC, so it is not a drop-in for anything.
how_it_is_fast: LeMac's universal hash keeps a 9 x 128-bit state. Each 64-byte chunk updates it with 8 independent AESENC instructions, one per wire, with the message words used as AESENC round keys, plus only 4 128-bit XORs. That is 2 AES rounds per 16-byte block ('rate 2'). On Ice Lake and Zen, AESENC and XOR compete for ports 0/1, so the design caps XORs at half the AESENC count and avoids long dependency chains. The rate-2 floor there is 0.0625 c/B, and candidates were compiled and benchmarked automatically during the MILP security search to find one that nears it. GCM's GHASH instead spends carry-less multiplications and reductions on every 16-byte block.
when_to_use: Authenticating large in-memory buffers (16 KB and up) on x86-64 servers with AES-NI, where you control both ends. In the 2025 corrigendum's rerun at 256 kB, corrected LeMac ran at 0.079 c/B against 0.321 for AES-128-GCM in AD-only mode on a Xeon Gold 5320 (about 4.1x), and 0.069 against 0.466 on a Zen 3 EPYC 7513 (about 6.8x).

As the MAC half of an encrypt-then-MAC design with a fast stream cipher, when GHASH or GMAC is the bottleneck. At 256 kB it also beats single-lane AEGIS-128L used for AD only (0.079 vs 0.195 c/B on Ice Lake) and Tiaoxin (0.123).
Keyed integrity checks of bulk data where unique 128-bit nonces are available, for the claimed 128-bit security. With repeated or fixed nonces, the paper claims security up to about 2^64 data.

Benchmarking AES-round MACs. The benchmark/ folder builds and times LeMac, LeMac-0, PetitMac, Jean-Nikolic, GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S, AEGIS-128/128L/128X2, Tiaoxin, HiAE, EliMAC and smac1x8 with rdpmc under one harness.
when_not_to_use: Short messages. At 1 kB, LeMac costs 0.285 c/B on Ice Lake, 3.6x its 256 kB rate. On Haswell at 1 kB it roughly ties Jean-Nikolic (0.460 vs 0.451) and Tiaoxin (0.494). zig-lemac's Zen 4 table has AEGIS-128L-MAC ahead at 256 B (40.4 vs 32.2 Gb/s).
Anything that needs encryption, an AEAD, or a standardized algorithm for TLS, IPsec or QUIC. LeMac is only a MAC, and this session found no standard or RFC for it.

Non-x86 targets or CPUs without AES-NI. The code uses only x86 intrinsics, with no fallback or runtime CPU check. PetitMac is the designers' pick for small cores (18.3 c/B on a Cortex-M4, using separate T-table code that is not in this repo). pauldreik/lemac supports arm64.

CPUs with VAES or AVX-512, if you want the most throughput. At 64 KiB on Zen 4, zig-lemac measured single-lane LeMac at 416.6 Gb/s, AEGIS-128X4-MAC at 439.7 and the 4-lane LeMac-X4 at 764.1. The parallel variants are only an unmerged PR here (#3, open since 2025-03).
Shipping this code as a library. The API is one-shot only, with no streaming and no verify or constant-time tag compare, and two correctness issues have gone unanswered (see gotchas).

integration.form: source-drop (single-file lemac.c or petitmac.c; the top-level Makefile builds lemac.so and petitmac.so only for the Python test harness)
integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and <immintrin.h>. The Python reference uses a bundled pure-Python AES (aes.py from boppreh/aes, MIT). The benchmarks need Linux, make, perf and optionally sudo.
integration.min_toolchain: GCC or Clang with AES-NI enabled (the Makefiles use -O3 -march=native). The code XORs __m128i values with ^ as a GNU vector extension, so MSVC is not supported as written. The paper used gcc 12.2.0.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AES-NI only. There is no ARM path, portable fallback or runtime dispatch. The benchmarks use getrandom, perf and Linux sysfs knobs.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From the code, the context is read-only after lemac_init and lemac_MAC keeps its state on the stack, so concurrent MACs sharing one initialised context look safe.

gotchas: The famous 0.068 c/B was measured on LeMac-0, the version with the message-schedule error. The 2025 corrigendum's rerun of the corrected LeMac gives 0.079 c/B on Ice Lake and 0.069 on Zen 3, so the gain over Jean-Nikolic on Ice Lake is about 39%, not 60%. The designers no longer claim 128-bit security for LeMac-0 (proven bound 25 active S-boxes, only 20 without the linear-incompatibility constraints), yet benchmark/LeMac-0* is still in the tree. Use the root lemac.c.

lemac_AU and lemac_MAC cast uint8_t pointers for the message, key, nonce and tag to __m128i* and dereference them. That is undefined behaviour for unaligned buffers and can fault if the compiler emits aligned loads. Issue #5 (2026-08-20) is unanswered, so pass 16-byte-aligned buffers. The code also assumes a little-endian host and whole-byte message lengths.
Padding appends the byte 0x01 then zeros, while the paper writes M||10*. Issue #2 (2025-03) asking which is right is unanswered. Check test vectors before interoperating with the Zig or C++ ports.

lemac.c and petitmac.c both define global, non-static AES, AES_KS and AES_modified functions, so they cannot be linked into one binary as-is. AES_128_ASSIST is plain C99 `inline`, which can leave an unresolved symbol in unoptimised builds. Verifying a tag means recomputing it and comparing in constant time yourself.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LeMac over libaegis, Rocca, Tiaoxin and AEZ when you need only authentication of long messages on AES-NI x86 and can pair it with your own cipher. At 256 kB it is 1.5-2.5x faster than their single-lane AD-only modes on Ice Lake. Pick libaegis, HiAE or intel-ipsec-mb when you need a complete AEAD, short-message speed, ARM support or a maintained library, and for a production LeMac prefer the maintained ports (jedisct1/zig-lemac, pauldreik/lemac for C++20) over this reference repo.
verified_claims_summary: Peer-reviewed ToSC 2024(2) Table 4: gcc 12.2.0, -O3 -march=native, in-cache message, rdpmc, most frequent of 1000 runs. It measured LeMac-0 at 0.068 c/B against 0.286 for Romain Dolbeau's SUPERCOP AES-128-GCM (AD only) on a Xeon Gold 5320 at 256 kB, about 4.2x. The 2025 corrigendum re-measured the corrected LeMac at 0.079 vs 0.321 (Ice Lake), 0.069 vs 0.466 (Zen 3), 0.128 vs 0.637 (Haswell) and 0.126 vs 0.414 (Skylake). The GCM baseline is 128-bit PCLMULQDQ with 8-block aggregation, not VPCLMULQDQ or OpenSSL. Its timed call includes key expansion and H-power setup, while LeMac's key setup sits outside the timed loop, which mostly affects the 1 kB column.
status_note: Stale: the last commit (2025-07-10) merged Frank Denis's extra benchmarks. The repo has 2 stars, two unanswered issues and an open PR from 2025-03. The code is CC0 with the bundled Python AES under MIT, and lemac.c is about 7 KB, so it is easy to vendor. For maintained code, jedisct1/zig-lemac (MIT, pushed 2026-09-25) adds 2- and 4-lane variants, and pauldreik/lemac (C++20, BSL-1.0) covers x86-64 and arm64.
